summary: Short demo of Redwood's model catalog, selecting open models for clinical summarization and triage. Discussed benchmarks, compatibility matrices (quantization/CUDA constraints), deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs VPC), and next steps to run a POC benchmark with sample prompts.
transcript:
Header: 2026-04-05 15:00 PT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Daniel Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Alex Martinez (CTO, Lifeline Clinic), Priya Rao (Head of AI), Samir Patel (Infra)

[00:00] Daniel Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we can see a full invite in calendar, I'm Daniel Park from Redwood Inference, i'm the AE, with Maya from our SE team. How's everybody doing?
[00:10] Alex Martinez: Doing good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see the model catalog walk-through.
[00:15] Priya Rao: Yeah hi, thanks Daniel, hi Maya.
[00:20] Maya Singh: Great. Quick agenda, we'll go through the model catalog UI, show how to pick open models, talk about the benchmark numbers we run, and then go into compatibility matrix—like quantization and hardware constraints—and then Q&A. Sound ok?
[00:32] Samir Patel: Yep sounds good. We're mostly interested in clinical note summarization and triage routing, latency needs around 200-300ms p95 for short prompts, and cost is a big consideration.
[00:45] Daniel Park: Perfect. Priya, maybe can you share your current stack briefly? What are you using for inference today?
[00:53] Priya Rao: Right now we have a small in-house setup on GCP, some TF endpoints for diagnostics, and occasionally calling OpenAI for complex summarization. We want more control over costs and to host private models for PHI. Also SOC2 is a requirement.
[01:10] Maya Singh: Got it. So two parts to the catalog—first the UI, then the compatibility and perf talk. I'm going to share my screen.
[01:22] [screen share begins]
[01:25] Maya Singh: So here is the Redwood Console, top-left is Model Catalog. We curate open models and show performance profiles—throughput, latency, token cost estimates, and recommended quantizations.
[01:40] Alex Martinez: Quick q — are the latency numbers synthetic or from customer workloads?
[01:45] Maya Singh: Good question. We publish baseline benchmark numbers using representative workloads plus hardware-specific numbers; we also show customer-submitted benchmarks when available. But they'll be a guide; we strongly recommend running a short benchmark with your prompts.
[01:57] Priya Rao: What's the process to test our prompts? We need to guarantee no PHI leaves our VPC during the POC.
[02:05] Daniel Park: For Private deployments we can do a customer-managed control plane and you can run the benchmarks entirely in your VPC. For Hosted, we have strict retention and optional redact hooks, but VPC/on-prem is the way to keep PHI in-house.
[02:20] Samir Patel: We might prefer Dedicated or Private. Can you explain differences real quick?
[02:27] Maya Singh: Sure—Hosted is easiest, low lift, pay-as-you-go. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity for predictable throughput and capacity isolation. Private is fully customer-managed control plane, VPC peering, and optional on-prem bundles for air-gapped. There are tradeoffs in ops and cost.
[02:43] [03:00] Maya Singh: Back to catalog—here's a view of 'open models' filter. You can filter by task, size, quantization support, and verified performance. For example, we have three variants of a 7B model—fp16, int8, and a quantized int4-ish variant. Note: int4 support can be model/hardware dependent.
[03:20] Alex Martinez: Does Redwood perform the quantization or do we upload quantized weights?
[03:25] Maya Singh: We provide recommended quant profiles and can deliver quantized variants where licensing allows; for Private you can also bring your own quant builds. We also surface which kernels are selected—sometimes we pick Triton kernels or CUDA fused ops, but occasionally the kernel path is suboptimal on older drivers.
[03:45] Priya Rao: We are using a mix of NVIDIA A10 and older T4s.
[03:49] Maya Singh: Ok, compatibility matrix will show per-model recommended GPUs. For A10s you get much better fp16 throughput; T4s may require more batching or use int8 paths.
[04:02] Alex Martinez: About the benchmarks—what metrics do you provide? p50, p95, throughput, tokens/sec, and cost estimate?
[04:10] Daniel Park: Yes we show p50/p95/99, tokens/sec, and a per-token cost projection based on cloud GPU pricing and typical batching. We also provide a raw CSV you can download.
[04:20] Priya Rao: That cost calc—does it include KV cache reuse and prefix caching assumptions?
[04:26] Maya Singh: The baseline includes common caching parameters; we also surface recommendations for intelligent batching and prefix/K-V cache reuse—sometimes transcription misreports as K-V cash in older exports—sorry, haha, bad auto-transcript—K V cache, yes.
[04:40] [04:55] Alex Martinez: Ha. Ok. Is there a compatibility matrix that shows quantization + kernel support by GPU + model?
[05:00] Maya Singh: Yes here's the compatibility matrix—columns are model, quant support, recommended kernel, GPU families, and known caveats. For instance, this open 13B model with llama-family arch supports int8 on Ampere but int4 only experimentally on some runtimes. We flag models with known hallucination regressions too.
[05:23] Samir Patel: For our use case, summarization accuracy is huge. How do you validate quality across quantized variants?
[05:30] Maya Singh: We run eval suites tied to prompt sets. In the console you can upload your evals and we will run regressions across model variants; Redwood Optimize will recommend models/quantization profiles that minimize cost subject to quality constraints.
[05:45] Priya Rao: Can we run Optimize on-prem?
[05:48] Maya Singh: Yes—Optimize is available as part of Private or Dedicated add-ons; it can run locally against your eval set.
[06:00] [06:05] Alex Martinez: Any examples of latency tradeoffs? Like 7B int8 vs 13B fp16.
[06:12] Maya Singh: Sure—example from our baseline: 7B int8 on A10 p95 ~120ms for 64-token prompts; 13B fp16 on same HW p95 ~210ms but higher accuracy. There's also batching effects: with batching up to 4 you get better throughput but higher single-request latency.
[06:30] Daniel Park: And routing policies matter—if you set a latency-first route we'll send small requests to faster smaller models and fall back to larger models for higher-quality long-form responses.
[06:43] Priya Rao: For clinical triage, we have many short requests; that suggests a smaller model optimized for throughput and tuned prompts.
[06:51] Maya Singh: Exactly. Also consider tokenization differences — some models have different tokenizer behaviors that affect token counts; the catalog shows estimated tokens per prompt sample.
[07:05] [07:15] Alex Martinez: This all sounds good. For POC we want a shortlist: two open models for summarization and one for embeddings. Can you suggest candidates?
[07:25] Maya Singh: Sure—based on your latency and accuracy needs: 1) 7B Llama-variant int8 (fast, cost-effective), 2) 13B Mistral-style fp16 (higher quality), embeddings: 1) small text-embedding-3 variant open model with 384-dim embedding that works well and runs fast on T4.
[07:48] Priya Rao: Are embeddings available as a separate endpoint and priced differently?
[07:52] Daniel Park: Yes, separate endpoint and per-unit pricing; we'll include pricing in the deck we send.
[07:58] [08:10] Samir Patel: Any limitations on model licensing? We can't redistribute weights internally beyond our VPC.
[08:16] Maya Singh: For open models licensing varies; we list the license type and any distribution constraints. For Private deployments you can restrict model artifacts to your infra.
[08:28] [08:35] Alex Martinez: Security — we need SSO, SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and an HSM integration for keys.
[08:42] Daniel Park: All supported. We have SSO, SAML, granular RBAC, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations in Private and Dedicated. We'll attach SOC2 and a network diagram. Note that some private options require a support plan.
[08:58] Priya Rao: Great. Can you show me an example compatibility row for that 7B candidate?
[09:05] Maya Singh: Yep, here's one—model name, recommended quant: int8, recommended kernel: fused-attn-v2, GPU: A10/A100, T4 possible but expect 30% slower. Notes: tokenizer uses byte-level BPE and tokens per clinical note ~120.
[09:23] [09:30] Alex Martinez: For the benchmark we'll want to run with our prompts and measure p95. How do we orchestrate that?
[09:36] Maya Singh: We'll send you a benchmark harness—a small script plus a CSV to run locally against the POC endpoint. For Hosted we can run it on our infra but if you want PHI-contained testing we'll provide the harness for you to run in VPC.
[09:52] Daniel Park: We'll also include instructions for smoke tests, and Maya will help interpret the raw CSV.
[10:00] [10:12] Priya Rao: Timeline—if we run a 2-week POC, is that typical?
[10:18] Daniel Park: Two weeks is common. First week: integration and short benchmarks, second week: optimization and cost-quality tuning.
[10:26] Samir Patel: In terms of costs for Dedicated, do you have ballpark monthly for reserved capacity?
[10:32] Daniel Park: We'll include rough numbers in the pricing deck; for a small Dedicated pool (2 A10s reserved) you'd be looking at X — we'll provide a tailored quote.
[10:45] [11:00] Alex Martinez: About the compatibility matrix CSV—can we export it to include as part of our internal procurement docs?
[11:05] Maya Singh: Yes you'll get the CSV and a PDF summary. Also linking to the model card/license.
[11:12] Priya Rao: One more question: does the console show which kernel was chosen for a given request? We had a previous provider where kernel mismatches caused huge slowdowns.
[11:21] Maya Singh: We surface kernel selection in per-request traces and in the model profile. If we detect a fallback kernel we flag it and suggest driver/OS changes.
[11:33] [12:00] Alex Martinez: Ok good. Are there any gotchas for quantized models like hallucination or factuality regressions?
[12:10] Maya Singh: Yes; quantization can change output distribution. That's why we recommend running evals. The Optimize rules will filter candidates that fail quality thresholds.
[12:21] Priya Rao: For the POC we'll need the following: model catalog deck, compatibility matrix CSV, benchmark harness, trial API keys in a VPC-enabled test env, and SOC2 docs.
[12:32] Daniel Park: Noted—we'll send those. Anything else?
[12:36] Samir Patel: A quick note about network: we'll need IP allowlists for the Hosted option if we test that path.
[12:42] Maya Singh: We'll include instructions for allowlist and VPC peering.
[12:48] [13:00] Alex Martinez: Great. On the integrations side, what SDKs do you have? python/node?
[13:06] Daniel Park: Python, Node, Go SDKs and a rest API. We'll include quickstart snippets in the deck.
[13:15] Priya Rao: How do you handle model rollouts and version pinning?
[13:19] Maya Singh: You can pin model versions per route. We support canary rollouts and automatic rollback based on error or latency thresholds.
[13:30] [14:00] Alex Martinez: That would help us avoid regressions during model updates.
[14:05] Daniel Park: Exactly. And you can tie regressions to evals so changes are caught by automated alerts.
[14:12] Priya Rao: Any prerequisites for Private deployment? Network, on-prem hardware minimums?
[14:18] Maya Singh: Minimum is usually 2 GPUs for redundancy for prod; we have an on-prem reference architecture doc we'll share. Also firewall rules and an endpoint for metrics.
[14:30] Samir Patel: Let's talk about benchmarks specifics—do you test with variable-length prompts to simulate triage?
[14:37] Maya Singh: Yes our harness supports sampled prompt lengths and you can pass a distribution. We'll return p50/p95/p99 and tokenized length histograms.
[14:48] [15:00] Alex Martinez: Ok thanks. I'm going to hand it back to Daniel for next steps.
[15:05] Daniel Park: Thanks Alex. Quick recap of action items and next steps: we'll send the model catalog deck, compatibility matrix CSV, benchmark harness, trial keys, SOC2 and network diagram, and schedule the POC scoping call. Maya will draft the initial benchmark plan.
[15:22] Priya Rao: Sounds good.
[15:24] Alex Martinez: Thanks everyone.

[End of transcript]

Notes: transcription has occasional auto-caption errors (K V cash), speaker labels approximate. Download links referenced: model_catalog_deck.pdf (sent after call), compatibility_matrix.csv, benchmark_harness.zip, SOC2.pdf.
